title: House names on record labels and Jack Pettis and His Pets
summary: He explains how companies used pseudonymous band names and says the Pettis recordings were under his name.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Do you remember any of the tunes that you made for Pettis?

Well, that's another thing Dick. See each one of those, each one of those big companies had what they called house names. They had a name called the Knickerbockers, they had a name called the Campus Boys, they had the Charleston Chasers, the Lads Black Aces, Bailey's Lucky Seven, Ted Wallace and his Campus Boys. Oh, they had about 15 different names, you see. And every band that recorded would record on the, for instance if you had a good band, and you were contracted to, to, to, to Victor. Well then you couldn't record for Columbia or O.K. or Brunswick. So what they would do, they would get the same band, see like, like Nichols was, was tied up, the Memphis Five was tied with Victor. The Arkansas Travelers was another one of them, Miffin made a whole lot of them. They'd use these different, what they called house names, you see. Now they might, they might have five or six bands recording under that, under that same name. So you don't know what it was yours, unless you could tell by, by what they were playing, if you remember the tune or anything like that. But that's some of the names that we were called. But there were ones with Pettis, they were Victor. He was, he was supposed to be exclusive, Victor. Victor. And the name of the band was Jack Pettis and his Pets.
Yeah, he used his own name on it.
Yeah, on, Now that's, that's, that's the only one, but the rest of them, I don't, and I don't have one of them.
